description: Prototype gallery concept: Museum Gallery Timeline.
title: Gallery Prototype B | Museum Timeline

hero.title: Museum
hero.subtitle: Gallery Timeline
hero.lead: This direction treats each life phase like an exhibit panel. It is the strongest option if images should dominate and if you want the story to feel curated, cinematic, and easy for visitors to browse.
chips: Clear room for captions and callouts

aside.title: How This Prototype Reads
aside.copy: Each stage becomes a framed exhibit with image, caption, and short narrative. This design feels less like a code graph and more like a portfolio installation or curated archive.

legend.label: Research spotlights
legend.note: Can scale into larger feature rows

section_heading.title: Sample Exhibit Flow
section_heading.copy: All entries use placeholder copy and temporary images. The goal here is purely the visual reading experience and pacing between image-led blocks.

rows.title: 10th Standard
rows.copy: A clean opening panel. Later this could hold one important photo, a short turning-point note, and perhaps a small caption about why this stage mattered.

rows.title: 12th Standard
rows.copy: The alternating layout breaks the page into memorable sections. This is useful if the real page will include certificates, achievements, portraits, campus imagery, or visual artifacts.

rows.title: College
rows.copy: This middle section can later become a major feature block with layered captions, special callouts, or embedded links into projects, labs, groups, or academic chapters.

rows.title: Projects During College
rows.copy: If you want a richer visual gallery later, this pattern can accommodate project screenshots, poster thumbnails, lab photos, or multi-image carousels without changing the overall structure.

rows.title: Joined PhD
rows.copy: The latest chapter reads like a final room in the sequence. Later it can widen further for publications, active work, posters, PDFs, and links into your deeper research content.

footer: this version is optimized for visitors who should first feel the story through imagery, then read the details.
